doc.title: Peter Appleyard interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, October 4, 2012

title: Benny Goodman's 'ray', and a night out with Ava Gardner in London
summary: Appleyard describes Goodman's trust and generosity, then dinner and a jazz night with Ava Gardner, and Goodman's anger at his disappearance.

story.theme_name: Working for Benny Goodman: the leader and his bands
story.community_name: Working for Benny Goodman: the perfectionist bandleader

blocks.x: closeness. Dick and Julia are so beautiful, people. But Benny encouraged me. I never got a ray, although I got one mini-ray once. It wasn’t for playing. I stayed out for a day and a half. I had the time off, but the last time he saw me was leaving the Dorchester with Ava Gardner.
And that got you the ray?

I got it. I came back and he invited me to go to this party after the Royal Albert Hall you see. He said, “Come on over, come join us.” I said, “Okay.” And I was the only guy he used to invite. You know he didn’t invite everybody in the band, just, it used to be me. I used to stay at his house in New York, in the penthouse, and he’d leave me there sleeping on the couch, right next to the office, with all the information, if I’d wanted to search through it I could see all his business. He trusted me you know. I never went anywhere

near it. I did what I was supposed to do. He’d take me up to Connecticut to the house there on the farm he had you know. And if he was going somewhere wherever he had to drive, he’d call me to drive him. And then afterwards we would go out to eat together you know. Anyway, we went to the Dorchester and I’m getting my fill of lobster and whatever, and this very familiar voice that I couldn’t recognize for a moment, a lady, said, “Mr. Appleyard, we were at the concert tonight and we enjoyed you so much, would you like to join us for dinner?” I turned around and it was Ava Gardner. I thought about it for about ten seconds, and I said, “Sure, I’d love to.” So we go to the table and she’s with a major film producer, and so we started to have dinner together and I tried to get her to have a drink, she wasn’t drinking, so I had a glass of wine I think. And then finally she said, “Let’s step out of here and go to hear some jazz.” So we went over to Ronnie Scott’s and everybody knew her, she was a real jazz fan. Blossom Dearie was playing. She didn’t like Blossom Dearie. But that guy, I never can remember his name, he was a drummer, he had a flute in the band and a cello.

Chico Hamilton, good. Yeah. Chico. And she knew Chico. So we hung out. So now it’s about three in the morning, so she said, “Let’s go back to my place.” How am I going to handle this? What kind of a time am I going to have with Ava Gardner? The first thing she did, she walks in her apartment, or house it was, she put on Duke, and she’s dancing to Duke. So now it’s getting kind of late after about two hours, the maid comes down and joins us. And she said, “Oh, it’s getting to be bedtime.” And I said, “Ava, I have to go.” And she said, “What?” It was probably the first time in her life any guy split after being with her all night. I said — and I was going through hell with my wife at home then, bad divorce. And I wanted to be straight. And I thought don’t come on to Ava Gardner. She’ll appreciate it all the more if you don’t, I’m sure. And I’m sure she did appreciate it. So she said, “okay.” And she went in the back and came back with some sugar tablets that she had, over-the counter things. She said, “On this tour with Benny,” she said, “you’re going to be tired a couple of times. Suck a couple of these to give you a little advantage.” So she takes me outside and puts her arm around me and kisses me goodnight and gives me her card. She said, “Please call me when you come back to London.” So I had to go up to Grimsby to visit someone, that lovely little girlfriend I had, and she was remarried and all that sort of stuff. I went to visit them. And so I came back, and I had been legitimately off you know. And so Muriel Zuckerman, who was Benny’s secretary, was waiting for me in the lobby of the hotel. She said, “Where have you been for the last couple of days?” I said, “Well I’ve been up to Grimsby.” “Oh,” she said, “Mr. Goodman has been looking for you” and “Oh, here he is now.” And he had a ray on. So the first thing I said, was “Benny, don’t look at me like that. I don’t ray.” He had the blackest of

eyes, that would scare the hell out of the devil. Anyway he said, “Where have you been for the last 36 hours?” I said, “I went up to Grimsby to visit.” He said, “Well the last time I saw you you were leaving with Ava Gardner.” I said, “No. I was there a good part of the night,” I said, “but I left and went on the train up to Grimsby to visit some relatives.” He said, “Don’t you ever leave this tour without me knowing exactly where you are.” And walked away. So I turned to Muriel and I said, “Muriel, what was that all about? I’m 40 years old.” She said, “He wanted to take you to the Ritz for dinner last night and you weren’t there so he had to eat alone.” But I really liked him. I could read him. And if I saw there was a mood there I wouldn’t go anywhere near him. When he came to Toronto to play with the big band, I arranged the accommodation at this lovely hotel that I stayed at, and they gave him Pierre Trudeau’s, our former Prime Minister’s, penthouse suite, for nothing, for the week. And I had an old Silver Cloud Rolls Royce and I drove him to work every night in the Rolls you see. Then his daughter came, Benji, who was a lovely girl, and I picked them up and brought him from the airport and all that sort of stuff. Anyway a couple of weeks later we were playing in Ames, Iowa and he called me and said, “Are you busy” so-and-so. I said, “No, why?” He said, “Oh we’ve got this concert in Ames, Iowa. It’s nothing” he said, “it’s just a concert, but I’d like you to do it.” So I got up to Ames, Iowa and it was one of these huge hockey rinks, about seven thousand people there, and he said, “Oh, it’s nothing.” The New York Philharmonic, conducted by Andre Kostelanetz.
